title: Lula Wins Historic Fourth Term as Brazil Markets Reprice Political Risk
dek: The incumbent defeated Flávio Bolsonaro with 51.8% of the vote, according to the electoral court. Investors reacted sharply as markets reopened, while the challenger rejected the result.
author: Meridian Newsroom

image.credit: Raimundo Teixeira Mendes; SVG implementation based on Brazilian law

keyPoints: Brazil's electoral court declared Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva the winner with 51.8% of the vote after all ballots were counted, according to AP reporting carried by PBS.
Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the result and requested annulment; the report says Brazil's electoral authorities announced the result.
Reuters reported that the real weakened roughly 12% against the U.S. dollar as trading opened and the stock exchange was halted after a sharp fall; the fast-moving quotes are not end-of-day levels.
body:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic fourth term Sunday, defeating Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff that has immediate implications for the country's political outlook and financial markets. The electoral court declared Lula the winner after all votes were counted: he received 51.8%, roughly 4.4 million more votes than his opponent, the Associated Press reported in coverage published by PBS. Bolsonaro rejected the result and sought to have it annulled.

## An upset with a market aftershock

Lula's win followed a first-round result in which Bolsonaro led, making the runoff reversal particularly striking. The election also lands in the middle of a broader regional shift in which right-of-center candidates have made gains. Lula, who has been critical of U.S. President Donald Trump's pressure and tariff policy, is expected to continue emphasizing Brazilian sovereignty, according to AP.

Markets reacted sharply when trading opened Monday. Reuters reported the Brazilian real weakened about 12% against the U.S. dollar and that trading on the country's stock exchange was halted after a large fall. Those are opening-session reports in volatile conditions; they should not be read as closing prices. Separate reports described investors' concern about fiscal policy, government spending and the outlook for debt.

## The governing test begins now

The election result gives Lula another mandate, but not a blank check. Investors will look for signals about how his administration plans to manage public debt while maintaining social programs and investment. Any sustained change in market pricing will depend on policy details and legislative support, not solely on the election-night outcome.

Bolsonaro's refusal to concede adds a procedural uncertainty, but the available reporting identifies Lula as the winner declared by the electoral authority. The near-term focus is on whether legal challenges proceed, how the transition unfolds and whether the government's first fiscal signals stabilize investor expectations.

marketImpact.summary: Brazilian assets sold off at the open after Lula's victory, reflecting investor concern about fiscal policy and uncertainty over the next administration's economic signals; the early move is not a settled close.
marketImpact.timeframe: Opening reaction on October 26 and the first weeks of post-election policy signals

tickers.rationale: Brazil-focused U.S. equity exposure may reflect the sharp local-market opening move, though ETF trading and currency effects differ from Brazil's cash index.
Reuters reported the real weakened about 12% against the U.S. dollar as trading opened; subsequent direction depends on fiscal guidance and policy credibility.
